name: Ghandruk
tagline: Gurung village of slate roofs facing Annapurna South
meta_description: Ghandruk guide: 1,940 m Gurung village 3 h by jeep from Pokhara, with Gurkha heritage, a Gurung museum and close views of Annapurna South.
summary: Ghandruk (1,940 m) is the largest Gurung village in the Annapurna foothills, about 3 hours by jeep from Pokhara via Nayapul and Kimche. Stone houses with slate roofs climb a terraced slope facing Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and Machhapuchhre, and the village has a Gurung museum and long ties to the Gurkha regiments.
intro: Ghandruk spreads over a south-facing spur above the Modi Khola, with several hundred houses linked by flagstone lanes and stone staircases. The old core, Ghandruk's upper village, keeps grey slate roofs, carved wooden windows and walled courtyards where maize dries in autumn. Below and around it, newer lodges with green roofs serve trekkers. Directly north, Annapurna South (7,219 m) and Hiunchuli (6,441 m) look close enough to touch, with Machhapuchhre's sharp summit to the right.

This is Gurung country, and Ghandruk has sent men to the British and Indian Gurkha regiments for more than a century. Pensions and remittances built many of the bigger houses, schools and the village's early micro-hydro scheme. The Annapurna Conservation Area Project opened one of its first offices here in the late 1980s, and Ghandruk became a model for community-run conservation, lodge management committees and trail upkeep across the region.

A road now reaches Kimche, below the village, so Ghandruk works as a short family break as well as a trek stop. We often plan it as a two- or three-day trip from Pokhara, or as the last night of the Poon Hill loop. Our three-day Ghandruk family trek starts at ₹19,000 or US$220 per person. Around 30 December the village celebrates Tamu Lhosar, the Gurung New Year, with dances, dress and feasting.
facts: Pokhara International Airport, ≈ 3 h by jeep
≈ 25 min flight or 6–8 h drive to Pokhara + 3 h jeep via Nayapul and Kimche
Gurung culture, Gurkha families, slate-roofed lanes, Annapurna South views

highlights.title: Old Gurung Museum
highlights.text: A traditional house in the upper village has been turned into a small museum of Gurung life: brass pots, bamboo baskets, weaving looms, shamanic drums and old Gurkha uniforms. It takes 30–45 minutes, and a family member often explains each object. Entry is a small fee, paid on the spot.

highlights.title: Annapurna South at sunrise
highlights.text: Ghandruk faces north, so the first sun lands on Annapurna South (7,219 m) and Hiunchuli while the village is still in shade. Climb to the viewpoint above the upper village at about 6 am in autumn for the best angle, with Machhapuchhre's summit catching light to the east.

highlights.title: Flagstone lanes of the upper village
highlights.text: Above the lodge strip, narrow lanes wind between stone houses, water taps, small shrines and terraced vegetable gardens. Walk slowly and greet people with 'namaste'; elderly women often sit weaving on doorsteps. An hour's loop gives a clearer picture of village life than any museum.

highlights.title: ACAP visitor centre
highlights.text: The Annapurna Conservation Area Project office in Ghandruk has displays on the region's wildlife, forests and community programmes, including the lodge committees and micro-hydro schemes that started here. It is worth 20 minutes and is also where rangers can update you on trail conditions.

highlights.title: Gurkha heritage
highlights.text: Many Ghandruk families have served in the British and Indian Gurkha regiments for three or four generations. Retired soldiers run some of the lodges, and photographs of men in uniform hang in many dining rooms. Ask politely, and you may hear stories from Hong Kong, Brunei or the Indian frontier.

highlights.title: Tamu Lhosar in late December
highlights.text: Gurung New Year, Tamu Lhosar, falls on 15 Poush in the Nepali calendar, close to 30 December. Ghandruk marks it with dances in traditional dress, feasts and visits between families. Rooms fill with Nepali visitors, so book early if your trip falls that week.

how_to_reach.text: Pokhara to Ghandruk takes ≈ 3 h by jeep: ≈ 1.5 h on the paved highway to Nayapul, then a rough dirt road up the Modi Khola valley to Kimche (1,640 m) and, in dry weather, on towards the lower village. From Kimche it is a 1–1.5 h walk up stone steps. Monsoon landslides can close the upper road; check current status before you travel.

Ghandruk sits on several trekking routes. From Tadapani (2,630 m) it is a 2.5–3 h descent through forest. From Landruk across the Modi Khola gorge, allow 3–4 h, dropping to the river and climbing back up. Chhomrong is 5–6 h away via Komrong Danda, and Nayapul about 5 h on the old trail through Birethanti.

Charter helicopters can land at Ghandruk's helipad in about 10–12 minutes from Pokhara, mostly for evacuations, tight schedules or guests at the Himalaya Lodge. Flights run in the morning before cloud builds and are cancelled in poor visibility. We quote these on request; check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Ghandruk has the widest choice of rooms on this side of the Annapurnas. Most teahouses line the main staircase between the lower village and the upper village, with Annapurna South views from their terraces; Gurung Cottage is a well-known family teahouse here. For more comfort, Ker & Downey's Himalaya Lodge stands above the village at about 2,000 m, with en-suite rooms and a garden facing the mountains, and is the Ghandruk stop on our luxury lodge trek. Lodges in the upper village are quieter at night than those near the road head.
tips: Stay in the upper village rather than near the jeep stop, as the views are wider and the evenings quieter.
Ask before photographing people in traditional dress, and expect to pay a small fee where dress hire is offered.
Carry cash for the museum entry, small purchases and lodge bills, since the nearest reliable ATM is in Pokhara.
Plan the Ghandruk to Tadapani climb for the morning, because the forest trail is steep and cloud often builds after noon.
If you visit near 30 December for Tamu Lhosar, book rooms at least a month ahead.

experiences.title: Gurung museum and old village walk
experiences.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, year round
experiences.summary: A guided two-hour loop through Ghandruk's upper village, with stops at the Old Gurung Museum, community water taps, a small Buddhist shrine and the viewpoint above the slate roofs. It shows how a Gurkha village lives today, beyond the lodge strip.
body: We start from the main staircase and climb into the old village, where houses are built of dressed stone with slate roofs and deep wooden balconies. Lanes are paved with flagstones and just wide enough for a laden mule. Your guide will point out the water taps where families still collect water, the community halls where village decisions are made, and terraces planted with millet, maize, mustard and potatoes depending on the season.

The Old Gurung Museum occupies a traditional house. Inside are farm tools, brass and copper vessels, bamboo baskets for carrying fodder, looms for weaving the woollen radi blankets, and objects used by Gurung shamans, known as pachyu and klebri. A corner remembers the village's Gurkha soldiers, with uniforms, medals and photographs. The family who look after it often explain items in Nepali and simple English. Allow 30–45 minutes and keep small notes for the entry fee.

The walk ends at the top of the village, where a viewpoint looks over the roofs to Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and Machhapuchhre. In late afternoon you see women returning from the fields with doko baskets and children coming home from school. Dress modestly, avoid entering houses without invitation and remove shoes if invited inside. This loop suits families and seniors, as the climbing is broken into short sections with plenty of places to rest.

faqs.q: Is the Gurung museum in Ghandruk worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you have 30–45 minutes. It is small but well stocked with tools, vessels, weaving gear, shamanic objects and Gurkha memorabilia, and gives useful background before you walk through the village. Opening hours are informal, so your guide may need to call the family to unlock it.

faqs.q: How much does the Ghandruk museum cost?
faqs.a: Entry is a small fee, usually in the range of NPR 100–200 per person, paid in cash at the door. Students and Nepali visitors sometimes pay less. The amount has changed over time, so carry small notes and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can we wear traditional Gurung dress for photos?
faqs.a: Yes. Several families and shops in Ghandruk rent traditional Gurung dress, including the women's velvet blouse, replica gold ornaments and the men's kachhad, for photos at a fee. Rates are agreed on the spot. It is popular with Nepali and Indian visitors, particularly around Tamu Lhosar.

experiences.title: Gurung dance evening with the mothers' group
experiences.summary: On many evenings in season, Ghandruk's aama samuha, the village mothers' group, performs Gurung songs and dances for lodge guests. The donation funds trail repairs, schools and village events, and the performance often ends with everyone dancing.
body: Mothers' groups, called aama samuha, play a big role in Gurung villages. In Ghandruk they organise clean-up days, collect funds for community projects and keep traditional songs alive. Lodges can arrange a performance in the dining hall or courtyard, usually after dinner. A group of 8–15 women arrives in matching dress, with madal drums, and sings Gurung and Nepali folk songs while dancing in slow, swaying lines, one hand raised and turning.

Songs cover farming, love, soldiers leaving for foreign service and the return home. Some are the rodhi songs once sung in the communal youth houses where Gurung boys and girls met in the evenings. Your guide can translate the gist. Halfway through, guests are usually invited to join, and children in particular end up in the middle of the circle. Photos are welcome during the performance, but ask before close-up portraits.

There is no fixed price. Groups typically collect a donation of NPR 1,000–3,000 from the lodge or the guests together, and every rupee goes to the mothers' group fund. Performances are most common from October to April and around festivals such as Tamu Lhosar and Dashain. Tell us in advance and we will ask your lodge to arrange it; in quiet weeks, or when the women are busy with the harvest, the group may not be available.

faqs.a: An aama samuha is a village mothers' group. In Gurung villages like Ghandruk these groups raise funds, manage clean-ups, support schools and run cultural programmes. Their song and dance evenings for trekkers are one of their main sources of income, and donations go straight into the group's community fund.

faqs.q: How much should we donate for the dance?
faqs.a: A donation of NPR 1,000–3,000 for the whole group of guests is normal, more for large parties. Many lodges collect it on your behalf. Add a little extra if your group joins in for a long time or takes many photos; the money funds village projects.

faqs.q: Is the cultural show arranged every night?
faqs.a: No. Performances depend on demand and on the women's farm work, so they are most likely from October to April, on weekends and around festivals. Give your guide a day's notice. In June to August, during rice planting, shows are rare.

experiences.title: Forest hike from Ghandruk to Tadapani
experiences.summary: The climb from Ghandruk to Tadapani gains about 690 m through dense rhododendron and oak forest to a ridge-top lodge stop at 2,630 m facing Annapurna South and Machhapuchhre. It works as a day hike or as the link to Ghorepani.
body: The trail leaves the top of Ghandruk past the last houses and fields, crosses a small stream, then enters forest. For the next three hours you climb steadily on stone steps and earth paths under rhododendron, oak and maple, with a couple of small tea shops around Bhaisi Kharka on the way. Grey langur monkeys are common in the canopy, and in spring the trail is carpeted with fallen red rhododendron petals.

Tadapani (2,630 m) means 'far water' in Nepali, a reminder that the village once had to carry water from a long way off. Today it is a cluster of half a dozen lodges on a forested saddle. Its terraces face Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and Machhapuchhre at close range, and at sunrise the peaks glow above the dark forest. Many Poon Hill treks stay a night here between Ghorepani and Ghandruk.

As a day hike, leave Ghandruk by 7:30 am, reach Tadapani by about 11 am for tea and lunch, and descend by early afternoon. The forest stays muddy and leech-ridden in monsoon and can hold snow in January and February. Our guides carry a first aid kit and keep the pace easy, since the steady 690 m climb is harder than it looks on a map. Walking poles are useful for the descent.

faqs.q: How long is the walk from Ghandruk to Tadapani?
faqs.a: Allow 3–3.5 hours uphill from Ghandruk (1,940 m) to Tadapani (2,630 m), and 2–2.5 hours back down. The trail climbs about 690 m through forest, with a couple of tea stops. It is a moderate walk that most regular hikers manage without difficulty.

Yes. Tadapani has a small cluster of teahouse lodges with basic twin rooms, shared toilets and dining halls facing Annapurna South and Machhapuchhre. It is a common overnight stop between Ghorepani and Ghandruk. Rooms fill in October and April, so we book ahead.

faqs.q: Are there leeches on the Ghandruk to Tadapani trail?
faqs.a: In the monsoon months, June to September, yes, leeches are common in the damp forest. Wear long trousers tucked into socks, use leech socks or salt, and check your legs at rest stops. From October to May leeches are rare and the trail is much more pleasant.

faqs.q: How do I reach Ghandruk from Pokhara?
faqs.a: By jeep it takes about 3 hours: 1.5 hours to Nayapul on the highway, then a rough road to Kimche and up towards the village. From Kimche the final stretch is a 1–1.5 hour walk on stone steps if the upper road is closed. Shared and private jeeps both run; check current status before you travel.

Ghandruk sits at about 1,940 m, with the upper village a little higher and the Himalaya Lodge around 2,000 m. That is low enough for anyone without serious health issues and comfortable for children and seniors. Nights in winter drop to around 2–5 °C, with frost on clear mornings.

faqs.q: Is Ghandruk good for a family trip?
faqs.a: Yes. It is one of the easiest Himalayan village stays in Nepal, with road access, short walks, low altitude and plenty of lodges. Our three-day Ghandruk family trek from Pokhara starts at ₹19,000 or US$220 per person and keeps daily walking to about 3–5 hours.

Ghandruk is known for its Gurung culture, generations of Gurkha soldiers, slate-roofed stone houses and close views of Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and Machhapuchhre. It also hosted one of the first Annapurna Conservation Area Project offices and is a regular stop on the Poon Hill and Annapurna Base Camp treks.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Ghandruk?
faqs.a: Yes. Ghandruk lies inside the Annapurna Conservation Area, so foreigners need the ACAP permit at NPR 3,000, and SAARC nationals including Indians pay NPR 1,000. Permits are checked at the Kimche or Birethanti checkpoint. Licensed-guide rules also apply to foreigners; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is Tamu Lhosar in Ghandruk?
faqs.a: Tamu Lhosar, the Gurung New Year, falls on 15 Poush in the Nepali calendar, which is usually 30 December. Ghandruk celebrates with traditional dress, songs, dances and family feasts over a day or two. It is a busy time for domestic tourism, so book rooms well ahead.

faqs.q: How many days should I spend in Ghandruk?
faqs.a: One night is enough to see sunrise on Annapurna South and walk the old village. Two nights let you add a day hike to Tadapani or a visit to Landruk across the valley. On a trek, Ghandruk usually gets one night as part of a longer loop.

faqs.q: Are there luxury lodges in Ghandruk?
faqs.a: Yes. Ker & Downey's Himalaya Lodge, above the village at around 2,000 m, has en-suite rooms and a garden facing the mountains and is part of our seven-day Annapurna luxury lodge trek, from ₹1,88,000 or US$2,190 per person. Most other lodges are simpler family teahouses.

faqs.q: Is there mobile signal in Ghandruk?
faqs.a: Yes. Nepal Telecom and Ncell both work in most of the village, and 4G data is usually available, though it slows in the evening. Most lodges also offer wifi. Power comes from the national grid with local backup, and charging is often free or about NPR 100–200.
